​1. Background​
​This paper outlines the design and development of​​an electric-powered, remotely​
​controlled vessel capable of a two-mile ocean race while carrying a payload. Under the​
​mentorship of Dr. Herbert Tanner, a multidisciplinary team of undergraduate and graduate​
​students focused on a specific technical area aligned with their expertise, ranging from advanced​
​composite materials to electronic control systems. Students maintained close collaboration​
​through conceptual sketching to ensure a cohesive final design.​
​Our 2025 entry utilized donated catamaran hulls from the College of Earth, Ocean, and​
​Environment. Notably, those structures presented significant limitations in buoyancy, reserve​
​capacity, and waterproofing, ultimately leading to water ingress that compromised internal​
​components during the race. For this year's competition, the University of Delaware team shifted​
​from repurposing material to a comprehensive engineering build from scratch. The 2026​
​platform is a custom 6-foot Deep-V monohull designed entirely in Rhino3D, Orca3D, and​
​Fusion 360. While debating the construction of a tunnel planning hull, we ultimately opted for a​
​shape with enhanced wave-piercing ability and stability, taking into account the rough water​
​conditions from the previous year. To manufacture this complex curvature, we looked towards​
​the University’s Center for Composite Materials to produce a lightweight, advanced composite​
​vessel. Due to the significantly different naval architecture and scale of the new hull, the​
​propulsion system, steering, high-voltage power management, cooling system, and remote​
​navigation have been redesigned to accommodate a high-performance 8800W powertrain. By​
​moving to a custom build, we eliminated the geometric constraints of previous years, allowing​
​for optimized component integration, a significantly higher power-to-weight ratio, and the​
​structural integrity required to survive high-speed open-water conditions.​

​Figure 1:​​The Delaware Dynamos working during a weekly​​team meeting.​

​2. Design and Analysis​
​2.1 Hull Form Selection & Stability​

​Following a technical session with Professor Michael DeLorme from the Stevens Institute of​
​Technology, the team selected a Deep-V monohull configuration. This choice was driven by the​
​need for high-speed stability and the ability to mitigate slamming impacts at racing velocities.​
​At low speeds, a Deep-V hull sits deep in the water, which can induce roll instability due to the​
​elevated center of gravity created by heavy battery placement. However, as the craft accelerates​
​and transitions into a planing state, the hydrodynamic lift shifts the craft onto the aft section of​
​the hull. The sharp 29-degree dead rise acts as a cutting edge, slicing through waves rather than​
​bouncing over the surface. This reduces the peak vertical acceleration (G-loading) during wave​
​impacts, protecting internal electronics from severe vibrational shock while minimizing wetted​
​surface area to reduce drag.​
​2.2 Hydrodynamic Simulation & Drag Calculation​

​To validate the hull form and dimensions of our propulsion system, we performed a full​
​static and hydrodynamic drag analysis in Orca3D. Utilizing the parametric functions within​
​Orca3D, we iteratively manipulated key hull features—such as chine beam and deadrise—to​
​observe their direct impact on hydrodynamic performance and stability. We conducted a​
​comprehensive hydrostatic simulation with a 120 lb load to confirm the hull’s sufficient load​
​capacity and buoyancy for the 2026 payload​​Figure​​2​. To accommodate this increased load​
​while maintaining high-speed efficiency, the hull was designed with a greater-than-average​
​height, which directly informed the selection of a sharp 29.12° deadrise. Using the standard drag​
​equation, the force required to propel the vessel was calculated:​

​2.3 Hull CAD Design​

          ​The upper portion of the hull was developed within Fusion 360 with a focus on​
​aerodynamic efficiency and component integration​​Figures​​4 & 5​. Given the high target​
 ​velocity, the superstructure was designed to be as aerodynamically streamlined as possible to​

pages.text:
​section of the hull to house the outboard motor and its custom swivel-type retractable mount.​
​This design choice mimics the engine well or transom notch found in full-scale​
​high-performance vessels, which serves to anchor the propulsion subsystem deeper into the​
​primary structure of the hull. By recessing the mount into this notch, we achieve a more rigid​
​mechanical connection that effectively handles the extreme torque generated by the brushless​
​motor while simultaneously lowering the center of gravity. Furthermore, this configuration​
​ensures the entire propulsion unit remains a stable, modular subsystem that is easy to access for​
​maintenance or mechanical adjustments.​
​To further optimize the vessel's performance during the transition from displacement to​
​planing, a reverse chine was integrated into the bottom hull to serve two critical functions. By​
​redirecting the flow of water downward at the edges of the hull, the reverse chine generates​
​additional hydrodynamic lift, which allows the 120 lb vessel to reach a stable planing state more​
​efficiently. Additionally, the chine provides effective spray control by deflecting water away​
​from the hull, reducing the wetted surface area and preventing water from interfering with the​
​streamlined profile of the upper hull sections.​

​Figures 4 & 5:​​CAD models of the finalized hull design.​

​3. Power Management​
​3.1 Power Systems​

​To achieve our target speed, we required substantially more power than last year. For​
​batteries, we selected​​two LiperiAir 26.4V, 30Ah Lithium​​Polymer (LiPo) packs wired in series,​
​providing 52.8V.​​LiPo batteries were selected due​​to their high discharge rates and superior​
​energy density compared to traditional marine batteries. This voltage also allows us to run our​
​250 KV Flipsky 70165 motor at 13000 RPM. This motor was selected for its IP67 waterproof​
​rating and suitability for ocean racing.​
​To isolate critical control systems from the high-voltage noise and voltage drops of the primary​
​drive motor, a dedicated 7Ah auxiliary pack was integrated. This pack independently powers the​
​autonomous controller, linear steering actuator, and water-cooling pumps. The entire electrical​
​architecture, including power distribution, signal routing, and safety contactors, was mapped and​
​validated using custom KiCad schematics.​
​3.2 Thermal Management​

​A critical failure point in high-performance electric marine applications is thermal​
​overload. The Flipsky outboard motor runs at 13,000 RPM and draws significant current,​
​generating substantial heat. Rather than building a water-cooling system for the motor, we opted​
​to submerge the IP67-rated hardware underwater in a custom pod design. The pod has inlets for​
​current to flow through, effectively discharging the heat the motor generates through convective​
​heat transfer. This system also feeds seawater to dedicated auxiliary pumps that run fluid into the​
​Electronic Speed Controller (ESC) and batteries within the hull before ejecting it. This design​
​takes advantage of the boat's velocity on water and ensures the ESC and motor remain within​
​safe operating temperatures, preventing component failure during prolonged load.​

​ultra-lightweight composite hull that possesses professional-grade surface quality.​

​4.2 Propulsion Mounting & Steering​

​The propulsion system for the 2026 vessel is centered around a custom-engineered​
​outboard motor unit that integrates steering, thrust, and thermal management into a modular​
​assembly​​Figure 8​. To optimize the hull's hydrodynamic efficiency and reduce parasitic drag, the​
​unit utilizes a steer-by-wire design that eliminates the requirement for a separate rudder.​
​Directional control is instead achieved through a high-torque linear actuator mounted inside the​
​hull, which physically pivots the outboard to provide precise navigation during high-speed​
​maneuvers.​
​Inspired by full-scale marine outboard motors, the lower unit was specifically designed to​
​generate hydrodynamic lift. This lift-generating geometry, combined with a tilt arm that allows​
​for the fine-tuning of the motor's angle of attack, is critical for assisting the 120 lb vessel in​
​transitioning from displacement to a stable planing state. Thermal regulation for the​
​high-performance powertrain is managed through a multi-stage cooling architecture integrated​
​directly into the motor housing. Interior water cooling channels run through the lower unit,​
​utilizing the vessel's velocity to facilitate heat exchange.​

​5. Autonomy and Controls​
​Our autonomous architecture utilizes the Seafloor Systems AutoNav hardware, governed by​
​Mission Planner software. We retrofitted the system with an upgraded Here3 GPS module and​
​flashed the internal flight computer with the latest stable release of ArduPilot Rover. In addition,​
​developed custom logic to integrate thrust vectoring and autonomous commands with our​
​manual Radio Frequency (RF) control system.​
​We successfully established communication between the linear actuator steering, the ZTW​
​ESC, and the autopilot controller using custom parameter files. Preliminary waypoint testing in​
​2025 confirmed that the vessel can accurately track GPS routes, with ongoing​
​Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) tuning used to refine steering response and minimize​
​cross-track error.​

​have been implemented to ensure vessel survivability:​

​the entire wood core is skinned in marine-grade fiberglass and sealed with epoxy resin,​

​providing a completely water-tight, low-friction exterior. All internal electronics are​
​housed within IP67-rated enclosures, and wire penetrations are sealed with​
​marine-grade cable glands.​
​●​ ​Electrical Safety:​​The 53 V system requires strict safety protocols. High-current fuses​
​and contactors were installed to disconnect the circuit if current levels exceed safe​
​thresholds. In compliance with competition regulations, a manual emergency stop​
​(E-Stop) loop is integrated into the primary power circuit.​

​7. Conclusion​
​The transition to a custom Deep-V monohull marks a significant advancement in the​
​University of Delaware ASNE PEP team’s technical capabilities. Through the integration of​
​advanced CAD/CAM workflows, high-power electrical system design, and rigorous​
​hydrodynamic simulation, the team has progressed from component repurposing to a fully​
​engineered naval design approach. With fabrication currently underway and waypoint validation​
​successfully completed, the 2026 vessel is certain to achieve improved performance, reliability,​
​and operational efficiency.​
​While the final build and comprehensive field testing remain in progress, the team is​
​confident in its ability to deliver a competitive prototype for the next PEP competition cycle​
​2027. As a result, the team will not be competing in the current year. However, we intend to​
​present our design and development work at the competition to obtain critical feedback from​
​judges, industry partners, and peer institutions. This engagement will support the identification​
​of design limitations and areas for refinement, strengthening the overall system before final​
​validation.​
​Developing a vessel from the ground up with a limited team has presented significant​
​technical and logistical challenges, while also providing substantial learning opportunities. The​
​team remains focused on continued iteration and performance optimization, intending to deliver​
​a robust and competitive platform in the upcoming competition cycle.​
